subject: froala.com

verdict.headline: Froala was dismissed in one line, on licensing, before anyone looked at the product.
body: Two independent agents, on two different models, reached the same conclusion by the same route. Neither compared features, neither looked at price, neither opened the documentation. The decisive sentence in one run was six words long: fully commercial, licence key required.

This is not a product problem and it cannot be fixed with better marketing copy. The agent never got far enough to read marketing copy. It filtered the category on one attribute, whether a key can be obtained without a human, and everything that failed that filter left the list before evaluation began.

The same filter removed CKEditor and TinyMCE, so this is a category-wide dynamic rather than a Froala-specific one. Whoever solves it first takes the defaults for an entire class of projects, because the agent is not choosing the best editor, it is choosing the best editor it can finish installing alone.
Worth noting what the winner did not need: an account, a key, a sales conversation, or a decision by a human. That is the entire competitive advantage on display here.

One run makes the point sharper than the rest. It verified everything it relied on, but only against the npm registry and the code already on disk, and stated plainly that it visited no documentation site at all. Its entire comparison of the rejected editors came from memory. A vendor whose licensing terms live only on its own website is invisible to that agent: the registry metadata is the only thing it will read, and that is where the verdict is formed.

recommendations.title: Publish a key that an agent can obtain without a human
recommendations.body: A development or evaluation key issued automatically, rate-limited, watermarked if necessary, valid on localhost. The point is not to give away the product; it is to survive the filter that eliminates you in the first thirty seconds.

recommendations.title: Put the licensing answer in your package metadata
recommendations.body: Runs consistently read registry metadata and the installed package before anything else, and one read nothing but those. If the licence field, the README on the registry page and the package description do not answer whether a machine can get a working key, the answer is assumed to be no.

recommendations.title: State the licensing terms where the agent actually looks
recommendations.body: Both runs read the npm registry metadata and the licensing docs page, in that order, and neither reached the pricing page. If the terms for a free evaluation are not in the package metadata and the first licensing doc, they do not exist.

recommendations.title: Write the procedure for a machine
recommendations.body: An /agent-signup.md or /.well-known/agent-access.json describing, step by step, how a machine gets a working key. None of the ten editors we scanned publishes anything of the kind, so this is currently free ground.

recommendations.title: Answer the paste question in public documentation
recommendations.body: Pasting from Google Docs without garbage markup decided this task. The winner won because its architecture answers it structurally and the answer was findable. Whoever documents that answer best wins the next brief that mentions paste.

limits: Two runs so far. This is the first cut of a round that was compromised by a shared working directory and is being repeated in isolation; the numbers here will be replaced, and the direction of the finding is what matters at this sample size.
One task, one scaffold. A brief that did not mention pasting from Google Docs might have produced a different winner.
Two models from one family. Cursor, Copilot and Codex may filter differently.
The agents stated decisions and wrote code; nobody attempted to actually obtain a licence key, so the wall is reported as the agents perceived it, not as it would behave under a real attempt.
